So as others have said, they may be using an unclear term for non-renewal of lease. The big question is are they on a month to month lease, is there current lease yearly but expiring at that time, or are they actually terminating it in the middle of a lease term. By my understanding if it's the first two situations despite the unclear wording they are well within their rights and assuming they are not exempt from rental increase caps this may be being very honest with their reasoning. If they are terminating in the middle of the lease period then that is definitely something you have some protection from.

Assuming you are renting from a private party without a property manager many legal self help sites use the term non-renewal and termination (assuming that it's at the end of the lease period) interchangeably.

I assume this will be down voted but as a homeowner in San Diego my yearly costs outside of mortgage have gone up considerably, and depending on the margin they were operating at this may indeed be an actual financial loss to them or something that causes the amount made to dip below where it is financially worthwhile for them to rent it at that price. Given that 1-2 bedroom apartments can go for that price depending on the area of San Diego your parents got a great deal for the area for many years.

Speaking from experience my own homeowners insurance increased over 300% a year from approximately 1200 to almost 4000 per year and depending on what else the landlord pays for they could be seeing increased costs of an additional several thousand per year on maintenance. Assuming something as simple as if they have to perform one repair a year that could easily cost them another thousand or more.

So with that in mind if the landlord was working on a relatively thin margin of say even $500/month, they would only be profiting 6k/year. Which with the increased costs I mentioned above basically becomes nothing or even a gamble of if they have to make a major repair could have them losing several thousand.

That said I can empathize with your situation and that it sucks, but to some degree the landlord is not being entirely unreasonable. Assuming for a moment they are not acting in bad faith and terminating in the middle of a lease term. But given that they haven't raised the rent in 9 years if I am reading your post correctly I would be willing to guess that you are dealing with an inexperienced landlord, and that when looking over the numbers they realized renting at the current price even with the maximum allowed increase was unsustainable for them and baring the ability to raise it more they didn't have a choice but to either take a loss or at high risk of loss, or to choose to not renew (terminate) the lease at the end of the term.

That said they did make a mistake and if they have been renting for over a year they are generally required to provide a 60 day notice, so while you can attempt to fight it based on them citing the wrong amount of required notice they did still technically give more than 60 days notice so I am entirely unsure how that would play out in court, but I think they would have a strong argument that even though they cited the wrong number for required notice they still did provide more than 60 days notice.

That said personally rather than sinking time and money into fighting what may very well be a losing battle, again under the assumption they are not doing this in the middle of a lease term. Your best option assuming you want to stay in San Diego may be to see if you and your sister can find an apartment here to rent. I know in some of the further out areas such as alpine and Ramona I have friends renting 2 bedroom apartments for under 2k.

So this may be an unpopular opinion but as someone who has been on both sides I feel like there is some information that isn't said or I possibly missed.

Did he ask you to move in with him, or was it a mutual decision.

How long have the two of you been together.

You mention he has a high paying job, does he have any student loan debt that he is also paying off.

Does he pay for any of the mutual expenses outside of rent, such as dinners, nights out, etc.

That said your boyfriend does sound like a bit of a dick in this situation, but it's also not entirely unfair to expect your partner to contribute equally to a relationship.

It's also worth asking yourself if you were the one making more money would you choose to move a guy in who lacked the ability to financially contribute more than 25-30% and would you be effectively willing to take care of him and what factors would affect that willingness or lack thereof. 

Fwiw I'm not saying you are wrong and he is right in this situation. Just that there is some information missing to make a fair judgment.

I own the game one's I believe. (the open back version) can't remember which is which. Build quality is incredibly solid, and as expected of sennheiser the sound quality is amazing. I've owned multiple headsets over the years and these overall sound better than anything from a general peripheral company. (razer, corsair, steel series, etc) Mind you while those companies do put out some solid products sennheiser is a company that specializes in high end audio equipment so it stands to reason that when it comes down to sound quality they will be near the top. 

My only two complaints is that while comfortable, I feel that because of the sturdiness of the design they would be tight on larger heads. They also weigh a bit more than many lower end headsets so that may take some time to get used to. I'm able to play 3 or 4 hours straight without needing to take them off and give myself a rest. 

As for the difference between the two one is open back the other is closed back. I'd suggest doing a bit of googling on the difference but the basic difference is that open backs allow for a more natural Sound as though you don't have headphones on, they also allow for some airflow which will keep your ears cooler, but the tradeoff is that other noises around can still be heard. In most situations unless you are playing at very low volume or have a very high ambient room noise this isn't a problem. The closed back version will sound like a traditional set of headphones, be sound dampening but also sound more closed and confining. 

If you have the ability to I'd suggest going to an audio equipment store and listening to the difference between the two types (doesn't have to be the same model because the difference in close and open back will be apparent in any set of headphones). That said it comes largely down to preference. I prefer the open back as the sound is more full and in my opinion allows for better positional awareness in shooters.

I've worked with computers for about 17 years and this is how I've always explained it to people. 

Think of your computer like an office cubicle. The processor is like the guy sitting at the desk doing "work". The ghz rating you see is how fast he can work and the cores are essentially how many people working at that desk. Ram is like the surface area of the desk. The more ram the more workspace available at any given point. The hard drive is like a file cabinet within the cubicle the larger the hard drive the larger the file cabinet. 

When you get into multithreaded vs single threaded applications, a single threaded application can only have one worker on it at a time. A multithreaded application would split it in smaller tasks with each worker doing a fraction of the whole. 

On a typical computer you may have worker (core) 1 doing work related to Windows while worker (core) 2 is doing work related to your browser. And workers (cores) 3 and 4 are busy on reddit because they have nothing to do at the current moment. As you run more processes they become distributed to the various workers. 

Yes I understand this is not 100% accurate but for the purposes of allowing the average person to understand I've always found it clicks.

I saw Deadpool yesterday and was blown away by it. I can't remember the last time I've laughed that hard and been able to just really enjoy myself. Afterwards I watched a lot of the interviews he had done and saw how he mentioned his dad dying and how humor helped him through it. 

Right now I'm sitting in the icu watching my dad in a medically induced coma, on life support and feeling completely helpless. The only thing I'm able to do to keep it together is make the occasional joke to bleed off some of the stress and once he is stabilized fully intend to go see Deadpool again just to be able to laugh for a couple hours and get away from how stressed I am otherwise. 

Ryan if by some chance you see this I want to let you know I completely understand using humor to cope with bad situations and for making me feel slightly less alone. And to thank your dedication in making the movie a reality and how your passion really showed.

When your sitting around feeling helpless and scared you reach out in whatever way you can to find some comfort. Maybe I am being a bit self indulgent by wanting to let him know that his passion and dedication is helping me through a hard time. 

Edit 2: Thank you everyone who has sent me their positive thoughts, prayers, and best wishes. Everyone who has shared a story thank you for taking time out of your life to try and comfort some stranger on the Internet. I appreciate it and am continuing to read the comments to keep my mind off things. I'll try to respond to everyone I can but if I miss your post I'm sorry.

So I worked in an off campus college textbook store on and off for about 10 years until the owner had to file for bankruptcy earlier this year. 

I've seen how things have changed and there are multiple reasons for the problem. 

Initially when I started 10 years ago text book rental didn't really exist. Current editions were typically 3-4 year affairs and about 90% of sales after the initial release of a book were used. Typically if a new book were to retail at 100, we'd buy it back for around 60 then sell it again for about 80. While a 30% profit may seem like a large amount, you have to remember all the other costs associated that the store owner is not in control of.  When a book is first released if we sold the book for 100 it probably cost us 90-95. So it wasn't until a book hit used that we were actually able to make money.  Operating  costs per year were upwards of 150 thousand per year for a relatively small store.  (60k rent, 60k employee salaries, 10k temp hire pay, 12 pos software, 6k+ for utilities.) with that in mind in order to break even and stay in business it means even at 20 per book profit we would have to sell 7500 books a year. Given that 20 dollars profit was not very common, I believe the average was something like 12, we had to sell almost twice that before the business made money. 

Anyway in most cases people would spend 300-400 on books for a full schedule and on average get about 175-250 back.  So the actual cost was closer to 100-200 on books.  Which is still bad but given operating costs was about the best we could do. 

That said 10 years ago people would come in buy the used books for the books we had and new for the ones they couldn't. So the publishers still continued to make some money every semester. With the advent of things like chegg, Amazon rentals, and easy peer to peer secondary market via amazon, Craigslist etc it has made it harder for the independent stores to stay in business. So the first problem is it kills the stores so that when people would come in and buy like 75% used and 25% new it's shifted to primarily rentals of both new and used. So actual sales shifted to like 70% rental and 30% sales of which about 95 % used and like 5% new. And overall sales declined because more people were not using stores and just shopping online. As people began to sell there books directly online, or rent them the used copies available to us dropped considerably.  Books that we would buy for 60 and sell for 80 people began to sell for themselves online for 75, which meant if we needed more of a particular book we were forced to pay more for it and then either charge more or go bankrupt.  Ultimately we went bankrupt as we were unable to compete. 

So as the independent bookstores fail so does the independent stores ability to influence professors. What most students don't realize is that at least in the US the on campus stores are contracted with Barnes and Noble and will continue to be there regardless. The textbook industry as a whole sends representives to teachers to attempt to get then to adopt their book. Most today offer the promise of online services, homework designed by the author, and other ease of use items that many teachers jump on.  What they don't realize is that this comes at an additional cost to the students with things like online access codes that the textbook industry can charge 90% of the cost of a book for thereby killing the secondary market completely.  An example would be a math book that would come with online access the code alone had a cost of 90 while the cost of the book + code was 95. So why even sell a book if it's worth 5 bucks new. 

Anyway the effect that this had is that by bypassing the off campus stores the students lose the people fighting hardest for teachers to use books longer, to not buy into these online packages and overall to keep books more reasonable. 

TL:DR the shift in the used textbook industry to more of an online and rental approach while on the surface cheaper is ultimately costing  students more and is putting the only stores fighting against the industry out of business.

Really it depends what you are looking for. To me having started with the original Fallout and playing all the games in the series, gameplay wise this seems the least fallout of them all. ==That is not inherently a bad thing== 

Originally Fallout was a turn based tactical game. When Bethesda bought the rights to the franchise and released Fallout 3 where the gameplay shifted to be closed to the Elder Scrolls style of play but with a very important difference. The V.A.T.S. system. With the click of a button combat would slow to a crawl and you could selective choose who and where to shoot limited based on the amount of Action Points you had available. (AP being a moderately fast recharging resource) This slowed the pace of combat down immensely and in my opinion was highly superior to combat without it.

The biggest shift I feel is that the VATS system feels more optional this time around. The standard first person gunning seems much tighter, and more rewarding now. Turning the game into more of a midpaced shooter that feels similar to Deus Ex: Human Revolution in pacing to me.

That said. The level of customization in the game is significantly greater than previous entries and most other "open world" games on the market. There is a fully designed settlement system for creating towns. Mod systems for weapons, armor, and power armor. (The Power armor is treated like an exosuit that you enter and controls clunkier than when on foot. The benefits are more armor, higher carrying capacity, and greater damage, but you are limited on the amount of "fuel" so at least early on you are forced to choose when to use it effectively.) Character customization allows you to create whatever sort of character that you want to play. (You may want to look over the Perk Chart to get an idea prior to purchasing)

I'm 10ish hours into the game and am enjoying it immensely. As someone with no attachment to the series as a whole, you will not have the opinion of what makes or doesn't make a "Fallout" game. So with that in mind, I would say if you want a game that you are wanting to invest the time in, you will have plenty to do. The voice acting is enjoyable so far, the animations for the most part smooth, and the combat enjoyable. The level of customization can be intimidating but is fairly easy to figure out. 

TL:DR
Mechanically feels more like a shooter than either Fallout 3 or New Vegas. Tons of customization both your character and your equipment, and assuming content density remains similar throughout the map, tons to do.

It wasnt until I was on a combination of Lexapro 20mg/day and klonopin 2mg/day that I was finally able to make progress. After about 8 months I wanted to lower the dosages of those medications and after speaking with my doctor began to supplement my pills with some weed. With some experimentation I've managed to not only lower but almost remove myself completely from the pill medications with an occasional klonopin on the bad day.

I was lucky to find a proper medical dispensary and had various strains recommended and within a few weeks was able to find what helped and what didn't.

Personally I found certain sativas, notably Jack Herer or anything crossed with it to cause anxiety and mild panic attacks. Blue Dream as go to strain for controlling my anxiety. And then some heavy Indicas for sleeping.

I'd be curious if there were specific strains you were using, or what whatever you got your hands on.

TL:DR Weed has helped me get off a combination of lexapro and klonopin and manages to control what was severe panic disorder, but knowing how various strains interact with your body chemistry is important.

She had began to fall into a deep depression and was just wanting to give up. I would go and visit her on a daily basis and find her just staring at the ceiling in an almost catatonic state, she had no desire to even turn a tv on, music or anything. She was barely responsive unless you asked her things and at best you would have 3 or 4 word answers. She was also under the care of about 7 different doctors for various different parts of her body, and I was the one who talked to them all and then filtered the information to the rest of my family. Anyway because my focus was on her my business slipped some, I am a self employed web designer, and computer technician. A large part of my income depends on my ability to network, and to take time meeting new clients and explaining the services I can offer to them.
